title: The Last Time It Was Done
logline: Twelve times over fifty-four years a timber stockade was built on one piece of open ground to catch wild elephants and then pulled down again; the twelfth time was the last time it was done anywhere in the country, and the ground shows nothing at all.
human_question: If being appalled by something is itself a form of aversion, what was it that actually changed when a whole country was appalled?

place.what_kind_of_place: A clearing of open ground on the inland margin of a small low-country town, where a very large privately owned forest used to begin and no longer does. A stream crosses it, and in the bed of that stream a perennial spring comes up, which is why the place was chosen: the animals came to the water. Twelve times between the 1890s and 1950 a triangular stockade of heavy jungle timber was raised around the stream and the spring, wild elephants were driven inside it, and afterwards the timber went. The last of those twelve was the last one held anywhere in the country, and the practice was prohibited soon after it. Today there is grass, sand, scrub, the stream, the spring when the water is low, a marker of some kind, and — depending on which account is current — one or two surviving uprights of the stockade. Everything else is a date.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because it is the one location in this group that offers the camera nothing and has to be filmed anyway, and that refusal is the film. One frame, held far past the point where a viewer expects a cut, of open ground at a forest edge in flat mid-morning light: grass, bare sand, a treeline, heat in the air, a bird across it once. Then the water, which is the only thing in the place that is doing anything — clear over gravel, and the spring's upwelling in the stream bed, a small continuous disturbance visible only because the level has dropped. Then the ground itself at close range, motionless: sand, root, ant path, leaf. Then the opening frame again, unchanged except that the light has moved across it. The beauty here is the beauty of a long look at nothing, which is rare, and the payoff is that the frame never gives up what the voice has said happened in it.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, on purpose. Light crosses the ground over the length of a morning and the shadows of the treeline shorten and lengthen. The stream level falls through the dry weeks until the spring shows in the bed. Insects, one bird, a dog, a motorcycle behind the trees, the town's noise arriving in gusts and going again. The camera does not move in any beat except to be placed somewhere else between beats. There is no arrival, no event, no process, no work, and nobody performing anything. What changes across the film is only what the voice has put into the viewer's head, which is why the last frame is the first frame.
place.when_it_looks_best: Dry weather, mid-morning to early afternoon, flat high light or thin overcast — deliberately not golden hour, deliberately not dramatic. The stream has to be low enough that the spring is visible in the bed, which points at the dry months. Overcast is better than hard sun for the close ground work. A day with no wind, so the ambient track is thin and the held frames are genuinely still.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A study of one piece of ground and the water in it. Wide, still, long: grass going to sand, a treeline, heat. Then down to the stream, gravel under clear water, and the one place in the bed where a spring is pushing up. Then the ground at close range, the grain of it. Then back to the first frame with the light moved. It has a shape — the whole place, the water, the surface, the whole place again — and it resolves. Anyone who can sit with a landscape that is not performing gets a complete piece, and it is the quietest thing in the series. This is also the honest risk: sound off, this is the hardest film in the group to hold, and it earns its length or it does not.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same nothing becomes the only thing the group has that shows an aftermath rather than an act. The voice puts a documented occasion onto empty ground: a great many people did a thing here on a fixed date, saw what it cost, and then stopped doing it, and it has never been done again. Then it does the harder half. The sources place outrage, disgust, discontent and the wish that a thing be destroyed inside the same word they use for anger, and they say that word names something painful to whoever holds it first. And on the burning that comes after a wrong has been done they are blunt: remembering is not the fault, the going-over is, and the going-over thins nothing. So the film cannot claim that a country was cleaned by feeling bad. What it can do is say the date, name what the law did not give back, and hold a frame in which none of it left a mark.

sequence.on_screen: Mid-morning, flat light. One static wide held far longer than a shot is normally held: open ground at the edge of a thinned forest, grass going over to bare sand, the darker line of a stream across the middle distance. A bird crosses once. Nothing else moves. No aerial, no push, no rack focus.
sequence.voice: Twelve times between 1896 and 1950, a stockade of heavy jungle timber was built on this ground, wild elephants were driven into it, and afterwards the timber came down. The twelfth time was the last time it was done anywhere in this country. This is where it was. There is nothing here.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level, camera resting on sand, still. The stream running over gravel. Then a closer static frame on the one place in the bed where a perennial spring pushes up, visible only because the water is low. Ambient only: water, insects, a motorcycle somewhere behind the trees.
sequence.voice: It was built around the water. There is a spring here that runs all year, and animals came to it, so the wall went up around the thing they came for. Now take the old texts on their own terms for a moment, because they are narrower than the word we would use. They count exactly two minds of this kind. Both of them always arrive carrying a painful mental feeling, and they differ in one respect only: whether the state comes up by itself, or after somebody has urged it [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L9]. And the word is wider than rage. It reaches through grudge, fear, dislike and plain discontent [C007-M:L3].

sequence.on_screen: A second static wide from a different position, level, across the part of the ground where a line of uprights once stood ten feet apart. There is nothing standing. Dry leaves, a cattle track, scrub coming back. Held long, no movement, no music.
sequence.voice: On the tenth of August, nineteen fifty, a herd of sixteen was driven in here, without guns or drums, by around six hundred men who had been told to tap sticks against trees. A young bull came in with them. He was mating in the enclosure with two of the females, one of them the matriarch, and when she was noosed and tied to a tree he began charging the tame elephants sent in to help. He broke the hide ropes twice. He broke a one-inch wire. The tame elephants would not go in to him again. Releasing him was judged too dangerous. A rifle was found among visitors who had come in that day from a shoot elsewhere, and he was shot. You will not be shown any of that. There is no photograph of it in this film, no reconstruction of it, and nothing on this ground to point at.

sequence.on_screen: Back to the empty middle of the clearing, static, wide, held. Absolutely nothing happens in the frame for its whole length. The town's sound comes and goes behind the treeline.
sequence.voice: What happened next is the reason this ground is worth standing on. The newspapers ran it on the front page — preferred death to captivity, one of them said; shot while defending the herd, said another. Public feeling ran very high. It was argued in Parliament. A law followed, and the thing was never done again. Before you decide that feeling was the good part, hear what the texts put inside the word. Disgust. Discontent. Displeasure at not getting what one wanted. The wish that a thing be destroyed. All of them are the same factor [C022-P:L121]. And they say it works like rust in iron, which is to say it damages the thing it arises in, in this life, first [C022-P:L119].

sequence.on_screen: Close and static on the ground itself: sand, gravel, a root, an ant path crossing it, one dry leaf. Macro but completely motionless, and held. No hand enters the frame.
sequence.voice: There is a factor in the list for exactly this — the burning that comes afterwards about a wrong done and a good not done — and it is counted only inside those same two minds [C022-P:L149]. The texts are then very exact, and not in the direction anyone expects. Simply remembering what was done is not the fault. The going-over is. Many people, it says, treat that going-over as a virtue that thins the wrong. It does not thin it. It defiles the mind again and can make a small wrong heavy; and brooding over good not done produces no good at all, it only weakens the mind that would have done some [C022-P:L143]. So nothing that was felt in this country after that afternoon undid anything that was done on this ground.

sequence.on_screen: A slow, single, very gradual widening — the only camera move in the film, and barely a move — from the ground back out to the whole clearing. Or, if it cannot be done without looking like an effect, a plain cut to the widest frame available. Ordinary present use at the edges: a path, a fence line, a cultivated patch, nobody identifiable.
sequence.voice: One of the two texts lists the occasions when this state of mind comes up, and among them, alongside the death of a parent or a child, it puts this: when great wrongs have been done by one's own hand [C007-M:L19]. That is as close as the old books come to this piece of ground, and it is a description of a moment of mind, not a verdict on anybody who stood here. The men who did this were not doing anything unlawful. Shooting an elephant was licensed at the time. Nobody here got what they deserved, and nothing that happened afterwards was a reckoning.

sequence.on_screen: Whatever now stands on the site: a marker, a plaque, one or two surviving uprights, a monument if there is one. Filmed once, level, from a normal distance, in the same flat light as everything else. No low angle, no push in, no held reverence, no cutaway to a detail. Then straight back to open ground.
sequence.voice: He was given a royal title afterwards — this place's name, and the words for king of elephants — and a book and a song and a monument came with it. The eyewitness account written up by a man who had the story from one of the organisers says he was not a tusker and not the leader of the herd; he was a strong young male who had followed two females in. The film records that a title was given. It does not use it. Nothing here was heroic and nothing here was a sacrifice, and an animal shot in an enclosure is not improved by being crowned.

sequence.on_screen: The opening frame again, exactly: the same lens, the same position, the same ground. The light has moved across it and the shadows are shorter. Held to the end. The film stops on it without cutting away.
sequence.voice: The sixteen were still taken. They were sold at auction within the week, and every adult among them except the two smallest already carried old gunshot wounds from somewhere else. The forest is gone. The law gave nothing back here; it only stopped a thing being done, which is not nothing, and is also not repair. The older text ends its own account by saying that this is the state of mind ordinary people fall into most often, and that knowing it, one should live attentively [C007-P:L65]. A camera cannot see which state of mind anyone was in, and this film has never claimed to. It can hold a date, and a piece of ground that does not remember it.

concept_merge.why_together: C007 is the machinery and C022 supplies the one factor that only an aftermath can show. Read fresh, C007 is remarkably narrow: exactly two hate-rooted minds, both always carrying a painful mental feeling and aversion, divided from each other by nothing except whether the state arose by itself or after urging [C007-P:L25–L28], with the Margaya illustrating the prompted one through acting on one's own initiative against acting when urged [C007-M:L9], and widening the word to cover grudge, fear, dislike and plain discontent [C007-M:L3]. It then lists the occasions, life's afflictions and the plain refusal of what one wanted among them [C007-P:L49], and the Margaya adds, in the same list as a parent's death, the case of great wrongs having been done by one's own hand [C007-M:L19]. C022 puts the same factor inside its fourteen and spells out its range — anger, fear, disgust, the burning when what was wanted did not come, discontent, the wish for revenge, the wish that a thing be destroyed [C022-P:L121] — and says it does its damage in the one it arises in, like rust in iron [C022-P:L119]. And C022 carries remorse, kukkucca, the burning afterwards about a wrong done and a good left undone, counted in those two minds only [C022-P:L149; C022-M:L49]. On this ground the two stop being a taxonomy, because here there is a dated occasion with a recorded aftermath: an act, then a great deal of public feeling about the act, then a law, then fifty-six years of nothing.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the aftermath is not outside the subject. Every other film in this group can only watch the act or the arrangement, and C007 on its own describes a mind no camera can find. What this place adds is the second half of the sentence: a country was appalled, and the sources refuse to move being appalled into a different category. Disgust and the wish that something be destroyed are the same factor as the thing they were about [C022-P:L121], and the factor is painful to its holder first [C007-P:L25–L28; C022-P:L119]. Then C022 closes the exit that a viewer will reach for, which is that at least the remorse was worth something: the text says plainly that remembering is not the fault, that the going-over is, that it thins nothing and can make a small wrong heavy, and that brooding over good not done produces no good [C022-P:L143]. What is left, once feeling has been denied the credit, is the bare fact that a practice stopped — and a clearing with nothing in it, which is the most accurate available picture of a wrong that was not undone.

concept_links.why: The sources teach exactly two minds of this kind, both always accompanied by a painful mental feeling and by aversion, differing only in whether they arise unprompted or after urging [C007-P:L25–L28], and the Margaya makes the prompted case concrete through acting of one's own wish against acting because somebody urged it [C007-M:L9]. That division is the one the film can honestly use over a place where an act was organised by hundreds of people for months, and it is used as a category and never as an accusation. The Pradeepika grounds the factor in meeting something unwanted and wanting it gone [C007-P:L32–L34], lists the occasions, with not getting what one wants among them [C007-P:L49], and the Margaya widens the word past rage to grudge, fear, dislike and discontent [C007-M:L3] and puts, in its list of occasions, alongside a parent's or a child's death, the case of great wrongs having been done by one's own hand [C007-M:L19]. That line is the film's spine and the reason this location is not a stretch: it is the sources' own name for an aftermath. The digest's limits are carried on screen rather than left outside the film. The sources make no exception for the anger anyone thinks is warranted, and treat the aversion in killing something that threatens you as the fierce form of the same state [C007-M:L11], so the public outrage of 1950 is not offered as the acceptable kind. The Pradeepika's account of what this state does to the one who holds it includes bodily signs, and it makes a claim about where such a mind at death leads [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L51]; both are traditional teaching rather than observable fact and neither is narrated. Killing and harsh speech are named as fixed in this mind [C007-P:L53]; that is stated nowhere in this film, because attaching it to a documented act by named and now-dead people would be a verdict, and a camera cannot show which factor was present in anyone. The text's own closing note, that these minds arise most often in ordinary unawakened people and that one should therefore live attentively [C007-P:L65], is the film's last line, because it puts the viewer inside the frame rather than above it.

Among the fourteen unwholesome factors, hate is given a range far wider than the English word anger: anger at what is met, fear once the object is judged too strong, the shrinking of disgust, the burning when what was wanted did not come, discontent, displeasure, the wish for revenge and the wish that a thing be destroyed [C022-P:L121; C022-M:L35]. That range is what licenses this film to treat a nationwide outrage as the group's own subject rather than as a happy ending, and the same passage says the factor damages the one it arises in, in this very life, the way rust arising in iron destroys the iron [C022-P:L119]. The list also carries remorse: the burning that comes afterwards about a wrong done and a good left undone, its object always the past, counted only and non-fixedly in the two hate-rooted minds [C022-P:L141; C022-P:L149; C022-M:L49]. The digest's own warning on that factor is the most load-bearing line in this record and is kept exactly: the Pradeepika rejects the idea that remorse purifies, separating simply recalling a wrong, which is not the fault, from the going-over, which is, and saying that the going-over defiles the mind again, can make a formerly small wrong heavy, and in the case of good left undone produces no good but only weakens the mind that would have acted [C022-P:L143]. The film therefore does not convert 1950 into a moral about feeling bad, and does not tell an audience to. Two further limits apply. The four factors present in every unwholesome mind describe moments, not kinds of person [C022-P:L31], so they are never used to read the organisers, the village or anyone in frame. And not all fear is a fault: the dread of doing wrong is a different factor altogether and the sources praise it through the harm its absence does [C022-P:L63], so the film never treats fear as such as a defect.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That being appalled by something is not in a different family from the thing it is about — the texts put disgust, discontent and the wish that a thing be destroyed inside one word, and say that word names something that hurts whoever is holding it first. That the going-over afterwards, which almost everyone treats as the decent part, is described in the sources as thinning nothing and sometimes making a small wrong heavier. And that even so, a thing can simply stop being done: not undone, not repaired, not atoned for, just stopped — which looks, on the ground where it used to be done, exactly like an empty field.
what_must_be_real: The ground exactly as it is on the day of filming. Nothing is cleared, dressed, raked, planted or added; no timber is laid or stood up to suggest where a stockade was; no marker is placed and none is moved. The stream is filmed at whatever level it happens to be, and if the spring is not visible that week it is not filmed. The local observance around the spring is respected in full — it is held in regard and people there do not point directly at it when giving its position — and no resident is asked to demonstrate, explain or re-enact any of that for a camera. Whatever memorial, plaque, post or statue now stands on the site is filmed once, level, at a normal distance, or not at all; it is never the film's subject and never framed to be moving. No living elephant appears anywhere in this film: none is filmed, waited for, hired, visited or cut in, and no captive, working, chained or temple animal stands in for the story. No photograph, film, drawing, animation or reconstruction of any capture, noosing, restraint or killing is used, and if the only way to make a beat legible is an image of that kind, the beat is cut. Nobody in frame is an exhibit and nobody appears who has not agreed; no resident is invited to perform local memory, and no descendant of anyone involved in 1950 is approached for reaction. The narration's numbers, dates and sequence come from the published record, the disagreements in that record are either said aloud or left out, and nothing is smoothed. No community, caste, family, office or profession is characterised, and the people who held these events, who are all dead, are not judged.
position_hint: late in the group: it is the only film here whose subject is what came after an act rather than the act, and it is the coldest, stillest and emptiest thing in the group, so it works once the viewer has sat through the films where the heat is visible and can hear an argument about outrage without needing a picture of anger. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Any re-enactment, reconstruction, animation, dramatisation, archival film or archival photograph of the capture or the killing. The event exists in this film only as narration over ground that shows no trace of it; the moment an image of it appears the film has become the thing it refuses to be. Historical kraal photographs and colonial prints do exist and several are on Wikimedia Commons; none showing an animal being driven, noosed, restrained, struck or killed may be used.

Any animal suffering as spectacle, anywhere. No captive, working, chained, temple or orphanage elephant is filmed to stand in for the story, no park or holding ground is visited for 'elephant footage', and if a beat seems to need a living elephant in frame it does not get one.

Making the bull a martyr. Popular memory gave him a royal title, a book, a song and a monument, and the contemporary press ran 'preferred death to captivity' and 'shot while defending the herd'; the eyewitness-based account says he was neither a tusker nor the herd's leader. The film records that the title was given and does not adopt it, does not narrate defiance as virtue, and does not use the name as an emblem.

Implicating the village, the families, the organisers or anyone's descendants. The practice was lawful and customary, shooting elephants was licensed at the time, everyone involved is dead, and no living community is answerable. No family, caste, office or community is characterised; the landowner is named once in the historical record and judged nowhere.

Letting the ending read as a reckoning. Kamma is not fate: nothing and nobody here got what they deserved, the animal's death was not a punishment, and the end of the practice was a decision taken by people, not a verdict arriving.

Stretching remorse into a moral for the audience. The digest is explicit that the sources reject the idea that remorse purifies, and separate remembering, which is not the fault, from the going-over, which is and which thins nothing. The film may not end on 'and so they felt bad and did better'.
Presenting anyone in frame as an instance of a defilement. The four constant factors describe moments of mind, not kinds of person, and a camera cannot show which factor is present.
Narrating the traditional bodily signs of this state, or the claim about where such a mind at death leads, as observable or medical fact.
Treating all fear as a fault, when the sources praise the dread of doing wrong as a different factor entirely and describe the harm its absence does.

Drifting into a present-day human–wildlife conflict film. Crop raiding, fences, watch platforms, night watches and current conflict are out of this film completely; another idea in this group has that subject and this one must not touch it.

Failing sound off. This is the group's hardest film to carry without narration: the ground is doing nothing and the length is the point. If the water and the surface work cannot hold a viewer for the running time, the film does not exist, and no amount of scoring or movement should be used to rescue it.
Breaching the local observance at the spring, or filming it in a way that treats a living regard as a quaint custom.
Turning the illegal gem working reported to have altered the spring's flow into an accusation or a second grievance. If it is visible it is recorded as what is there, and nobody is blamed on camera.

Aerial work. It is not needed, a clearing reads perfectly well from the ground, and an aerial reveal would import exactly the treatment this film is here to avoid. If a drone is flown at all it is for one establishing frame and it needs its own clearance.
drop_if: The ground has been built on, landscaped or turned into an attraction — a museum, a life-size replica, a reconstructed stockade — to the point where the absence the film is about no longer exists there and cannot be kept out of frame.
The event can only be made legible by showing an image of a capture or a killing.
The spring cannot be reached or filmed without breaching the local observance around it, or the stream bed is under active gem working.
The film would require a living elephant in frame to work.
Access to the ground cannot be had, or the only available position on it is one from which the place reads as a monument rather than as open ground.

connections.note: Both films have wild elephants somewhere in them and they must not be allowed to converge; this entry exists so the separation is on the record. That film is a present-day nightly watch on a protected-area boundary, filmed in the dark from the air and from tree platforms, where people keep animals out of a ripening crop. This one is a single dated historical event and a practice that ended, filmed in flat daylight on empty ground with a mostly static camera, and it contains no crop raiding, no fence, no watch platform, no night work and no present-day conflict of any kind. No living elephant appears in this film at all. Its animals are in the record and nowhere else.

That film's manor of low doorways stands about seven kilometres from this ground in the same district and on the same family's former estate, and its own record already attributes the house's wealth partly to timber, gem mining and elephant kraals. The overlap is real and is useful rather than duplicative: one film is an interior of small rooms and colonial posture, the other is exterior emptiness and a date. They are in different groups, ask different concepts' questions, and share no shot. Neither judges the family; each names it once as record.
A built thing that fear left standing, and an unbuilt thing that an ending left no trace of. One film is walls and angles that survive their purpose; this one is a purpose that survived nothing.

Recorded only to stop a false repetition flag: that film uses the word kraal in its other sense, a thorn pen for cattle in the northern grazing country, and is about the order animals leave a gate in. No shared archetype, no shared animal, no shared group and nothing shot alike.

selection.reason: Replaces a working-site film with the group's only historical-event film. Eleven of this group's fourteen candidates were working places carrying no historical story, and a group cannot be a monoculture; this record was the weakest of them, a yard of damaged vehicles that carried the concept by resemblance only. The new film rests on a dated, documented occasion with a scholarly account behind it, and it is the one place in the group where the record preserves the aftermath of an act rather than the act. It is also the group's only empty film and its only wholly static one.

review.note: Rewritten from the ground up on 2026-09-25 and the body is entirely new, so any earlier verdict on this record refers to nothing. What it was: twenty-five acres of yard holding the state bus fleet's worn-out and smashed vehicles, carrying C007 by resemblance — a place where other people's refusals arrive as metal. It was replaced because eleven of this group's fourteen candidates were working places with no historical story between them, Chathura has ruled that a group cannot be a monoculture, and this was the weakest occupant of that cell: an honest industrial film that demonstrated nothing the concept did not already say. What it is now: one piece of open ground where a timber stockade for catching wild elephants was built and taken down twelve times between 1896 and 1950, where the twelfth was the last held anywhere in the country, where a young bull was shot on 10 August 1950 after repeated attempts to restrain him failed, where the public feeling that followed was argued in Parliament and a law ended the practice, and where there is now nothing to see. The historical binding is exact rather than decorative: C007's shorter source lists, among the occasions on which these minds arise and immediately beside the death of a parent or a child, the case of great wrongs having been done by one's own hand, and C022 carries remorse as a factor counted only inside those same two minds — so an aftermath is the sources' own category, and this is the only location in the group that has one on the record. The argument was then held to what the digests actually license: C022's range of the hate factor covers disgust, discontent and the wish that a thing be destroyed, which means the national outrage of 1950 is inside the group's subject and not outside it as a happy ending; and the Pradeepika's flat rejection of the idea that remorse purifies, with its separation of remembering from the going-over, is used to stop the film becoming a moral about feeling bad. Guards on the animal material, all of them written into the body: no re-enactment, reconstruction, animation, archival film or archival photograph of any capture or killing, so the event is narrated over ground that shows no trace of it; no living elephant in frame anywhere, and no captive, working, chained, temple or orphanage animal standing in; no monument, plaque or statue filmed as a subject, only once and level if at all; the royal title that popular memory gave the bull is recorded as having been given and is not adopted, with the eyewitness account's correction — not a tusker, not the herd's leader — held against the newspapers' 'shot while defending the herd'; the practice was lawful and licensed at the time and nobody living is answerable, so no village, family, office or descendant is implicated and the landowner is named once as record and judged nowhere; nothing is framed as deserved and the ending is not a reckoning; and an explicit connections entry separates this film from the group's night-watch film on a park boundary, with crop raiding, fences, platforms and present-day conflict excluded outright. Concepts unchanged, C007 primary and C022 supporting, both re-read from the digests and both sources read line by line for the citations. Commons holds nothing honest for this site and images are empty, with the rejected material named in the research note. Three of this group's films now sit in the same district, which is worth Chathura's attention even though the location itself is fixed.

suggested_location.name: The Panamure kraal ground (Panamure Eth Gala) and the Diya Bubula spring, Panamure

also_known_as.name: Diya Bubula
also_known_as.meaning: the water bubble: the perennial spring in the stream bed inside the kraal ground

also_known_as.name: Kraal Town
also_known_as.meaning: the temporary settlement of 1950, with its own post office and police station

suggested_location.region: Ratnapura District, Sabaragamuwa Province, in the Kolonne division of the low country inland from Embilipitiya, about 171 km from Colombo and 55 km from Ratnapura
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only location available to this group that carries a completed occasion rather than a standing arrangement. Twelve times over fifty-four years a stockade was built on this ground around the water the animals came to, and taken down again; the twelfth was the last one held anywhere in the country; an animal was shot in it; the public feeling that followed was argued in Parliament and a law ended the practice. That gives the film the one thing the concepts need and no working site can supply: the sources name the burning that comes after a wrong as a factor of these same two minds, and the shorter source lists 'great wrongs done by one's own hand' among the occasions on which they arise, so an aftermath is not an analogy here but the category itself. And the ground supplies the image without any help. There is nothing on it. Twelve times something was built and removed; the last time ended a practice; and the place shows no mark of either. A clearing at a forest edge, a stream, a spring visible when the water drops, and a date is the most exact available picture of a wrong that was not undone, which is precisely what the texts say the going-over afterwards leaves behind. It is also, usefully, a place with nobody in it: no work to romanticise, no participant to catch at their worst, and no living animal to put in front of a lens.

historical_thread.story:
The kraal was the stockade method of taking wild elephants: a walled enclosure of heavy jungle timber into which a herd was driven and then noosed and led out for taming. Katugaha's account describes it as triangular, with a wide mouth narrowing to a funnel and two timber enclosures inside, and credits its introduction to the island to the Portuguese; the Dutch continued the pattern, the inner enclosure was given up around 1800, and in early British times before 1833 the shape changed again to a plain rectangle with concealed guide fencing running forward from the front angles. Robert Knox, held captive in the Kandyan kingdom in the seventeenth century, calls the thing a Pound. Katugaha notes that these events belong to a country still largely under forest: an estimated twelve thousand wild elephants at the turn of the nineteenth century, and about three thousand by independence in 1948.

The site came into use through one man watching another's. In 1870 a kraal was organised at Labugama by Iddamalgoda Basnayaka Nilame and Ekneligoda Dissawa for the entertainment of the visiting Duke of Edinburgh, and Maduwanwela Rate Mahathmaya and J. T. Ellawela went to see it. Some time in the 1880s Maduwanwela, encouraged by Ellawela, went into Kolonna Korale looking for a place of his own, and the two of them chose Panamure, taking in the main stream that elephants came to and, beside it, a perennial spring — Katugaha wonders whether it held minerals the animals wanted. The stockade was built around the stream and the spring. Kraals were then held on that ground twelve times: 1896, 1898, 1902, 1907, 1912, 1914, 1918, 1922, 1924, 1929, 1944 and 1950, the list attributed by Katugaha to Sam Elapata Jnr's 1997 record in Loris.

The 1950 kraal was held on private land belonging to Sir Alexander Francis Molamure (1888-1951), first Speaker of the State Council of Ceylon and first Speaker of its Parliament, who had inherited the Maduwanwela estate through his uncle J. W. Maduwanwela. Building it was a substantial operation. The logs were cut on his own land; posts from the 1944 kraal were tested and the sound ones reused; only every other upright was fixed into the ground, so that the wall would give a little when an animal charged it; the uprights stood ten feet apart; every knot was checked; over a hundred men worked on it and tame elephants held the logs in place. A post office and a police station were put up and the temporary settlement became known as Kraal Town, with camps for the Molamure, Elapata, Maduwanwela and Muttetuwegama parties and one for the Governor General. As custom required, the blessing of the jungle deities was sought before the drive, with a mock stockade built and dancers and kattandiyas brought in to perform the ritual.

The drive used around six hundred men, and its most striking feature is a restraint: no guns, no firecrackers, no drums and no banging of tin cans were allowed, which Katugaha contrasts with practice elsewhere where animals were lost in the resulting stampedes. Each man had a stout stick to tap against trees; quiet talking helped; beaters worked in threes and kept a ring of fires burning at night and sang pel kavi; the food provided during the drive was strictly vegetarian; the herd was never allowed to stampede. Walalgoda Ralahamy was in charge of the drive and Sam Elapata was in the thick of it. The gate was opened, the herd went in, and the gate was closed behind it. The herd was of sixteen animals, with a few loners about outside. Two of the females were in oestrus, and one strong young bull went in with the herd.

Noosing began and went on without difficulty for a while. The young bull was mating with two of the females inside the enclosure, the matriarch among them. When the matriarch was tied to a tree he became uncontrollable and charged every tame elephant brought in. He was noosed and snapped the hide ropes twice; he broke free even from the hira gala; a man was put up a tree with a one-inch wire rope set as a noose, which caught only half his foot and stuck between the nails and which he broke with one kick, and which left him more irritated than before. Many tame elephants refused to face him. Three were finally sent in, among them the Mapitigama tusker, and in the account Katugaha quotes from Sam Elapata Jnr the Mapitigama tusker turned its back, was gored in the hindquarters and fled screaming; a second fled; and only Gunaya, his father's animal, stood up to the wild bull, was pushed sideways on the head-on clash, thrust in the shoulder and knocked down, with the wild bull standing over it before Sir Francis came up with his charmed stick and drove him off. Releasing the bull was considered and rejected: a mating bull would not have left the area, and thousands of visitors as well as the beaters were there. Sir Francis decided to have him shot. No firearms were allowed in Kraal Town, and while he was considering asking the police to do it, Sam Kadirgama, Arthur Molamure and Shelton Ratwatte arrived at Panamure on their way back from a shoot; Kadirgama had a rifle powerful enough and shot the bull as it charged towards him. The hind legs buckled first, which Katugaha reads as evidence the bullet had reached the brain, then the forelegs, and the animal rolled over. Popular accounts date the shooting to 10 August 1950, with 9 August also given.

What followed the shooting is the part of the record that matters most here, and the part the scholarly account treats most coolly. The newspapers, Katugaha writes, screamed 'Tusker shot while defending the herd'; a front-page headline of the time is reported as 'Preferred Death to Captivity'. He corrects both flatly: 'it was not a tusker nor was he the leader of the herd. He was just a strong male that had joined the herd because of his sexual desires.' He also records that shooting elephants was not banned at the time and was done under licence in defence of crops and for sport. Then: 'There was much agitation about the "unnecessary deaths" caused by these kraals and public opinion ran high. Finally Parliament decided and passed a law banning elephant Kraals.' And, at the end of the paper, with an audible dryness: 'All this hue and cry that was made on the death of one animal. The emotions expressed and the debates in Parliament about this unfortunate incident, finally led to the ban on Kraals, capture and killing of elephants. Considering the fast declining number of elephants in the wild this ban came at the correct time.'

The captured animals were not released. Katugaha records that noosing finished, the captives strained at their bonds, and the next event was a public auction at which owners came from far and wide to buy, a purchaser being expected to take his animal away within five or six days. He also records, in one sentence and without comment, that every adult elephant captured during the kraal except the two tiny babies had gunshot injuries. Two other incidents he sets down: an adult female charged Sam Elapata inside the stockade with her trunk curled under her chin, the sign of a real charge rather than a mock one, and he got behind an upright in time; and on another occasion an enraged female charged Sam Elapata and the Governor General, Lord Soulbury, inside the stockade, and Elapata pushed Soulbury into a deep ditch and jumped in after him.

Sir Francis Molamure died on 25 January 1951, a few months after the kraal, after a stroke suffered while presiding over Parliament. The bull was given, afterwards and in popular memory, a royal title compounded from the place name and the words for king of elephants, and books, a song and a memorial followed. Katugaha's own closing lines are about the ground: 'Panamure is but a memory now. Gone are the elephants, bear, leopards and all the other smaller animals that roamed free in these jungles. The jungle itself is no more. Panamure is a developing town today. Just one or perhaps two of the upright post of the stockade are left and preserved in this town as historical mementos.'

The spring is still there, and still regarded. Local accounts hold that when elephants gathered at the Diya Bubula and trumpeted, the flow increased, and that the same happened when people came near and spoke loudly; villagers would not point directly at it when indicating where it was. It lies within the stream bed and is clearly visible only when the water drops, and illegal gem working and a diverted stream are reported to have reduced its natural discharge. It is reached by walking across the kraal ground to the stream and then about seventy metres upstream, taking the left branch at a Y and crossing one small tributary.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C007 and C022 describe one factor, and the whole difficulty of filming it is that it is invisible and instantaneous. Every other location in this group can therefore only show the standing arrangement in which it arises — a boundary, a queue, a delay, a watch. This ground offers the one thing an arrangement cannot: a completed occasion, with a date, in which a great many people did something, were shown what it cost, and then stopped. The sources have a name for that second half, and it is inside the same two minds as the first. That is the binding, and it works in four moves.

First, the sources' own list of occasions reaches the aftermath directly. The Margaya's list of when these minds arise runs through hearing one's own fault spoken of, a servant's disobedience, a thing asked for and refused, and then, in the same sentence as the death of a parent or a child, 'when great wrongs have been done by one's own hand'. That is not an analogy applied to 1950; it is the category the record fell into. And the Pradeepika names remorse — the burning afterwards about a wrong done and a good left undone — as a factor that arises only in these two minds, with C022 repeating that it is counted there and nowhere else. So the film is not importing an aftermath into a concept about anger; it is filming the one part of the concept that requires an aftermath to exist.

Second, the record forces the film to be honest about the outrage, which is the thing a documentary would ordinarily use as its resolution. Katugaha's paper hands it over in the plainest terms — 'much agitation', 'public opinion ran high', debates in Parliament, a law — and also, in the same breath, 'All this hue and cry that was made on the death of one animal.' The sources are narrower still. C022 puts disgust, discontent, displeasure at not getting what one wanted, and the wish that a thing be destroyed inside the single word for hate, and says the factor works like rust arising in iron, which destroys the iron. So the national feeling of 1950 is not outside the group's subject; it is the group's subject, arriving for once in a form the historical record actually preserves, and felt first by the people holding it. A film that let the outrage stand as virtue would be contradicting both the concept and the source.

Third, the sources close off the moral that this material is almost designed to produce. The obvious ending — they felt bad, therefore they changed, therefore feeling bad is good — is refused by the Pradeepika in terms. Remembering a wrong is not the fault. The going-over is. And the going-over does not thin the wrong; it defiles the mind again and can make a formerly small wrong heavy, while brooding over good left undone produces no good at all and only weakens the mind that would have done some. That is a doctrinal claim about a mental factor, not an instruction to an audience, and the film states it as such. What it leaves standing is much smaller and much stranger than a moral: the practice stopped. Not because feeling repaired anything, but because it was not done again.

Fourth, the ground itself finishes the argument, and this is why the location is the film rather than its setting. Twelve times something was built here and taken down; the twelfth ended a practice; and there is nothing here. Nothing was returned. The sixteen were sold at auction within the week. Every adult taken except the two smallest already carried old gunshot wounds from elsewhere, which is the record's own quiet note that the thing the law stopped was not the only thing being done. The forest is gone. The clearing is the most accurate available image of a wrong that was not undone, which is precisely what the sources say remorse leaves behind. And because the ground shows nothing, the film cannot become a monument, cannot make the animal a hero, and cannot adjudicate anybody. The people who did this are dead, what they did was lawful and licensed, and the only thing the camera can honestly hold is a date and an empty field. That refusal is also the guard the concept requires: a camera cannot see which mental factor was present in anyone, and here there is nobody in frame to be wrong about.
what_is_certain: Elephant kraals were held at this site twelve times: 1896, 1898, 1902, 1907, 1912, 1914, 1918, 1922, 1924, 1929, 1944 and 1950. The list is identical in Katugaha (Gajah 29, 2008), who attributes it to Sam Elapata Jnr, 'Elephant kraals at Panamure - A historical record', Loris 21: 118-125 (1997), in Widyarathne's 2016 Kelaniya paper, and in the popular sources.
The 1950 kraal was the last elephant kraal held in the country.

It was held on private land belonging to Sir Alexander Francis Molamure (born 2 July 1888, died 25 January 1951), first Speaker of the State Council of Ceylon and first Speaker of the Parliament of Ceylon, who had inherited the Maduwanwela estate through his uncle J. W. Maduwanwela. He organised the kraal and he decided that the bull should be shot. He died of a stroke suffered while presiding over Parliament a few months later.

The site was selected in the 1880s by Maduwanwela Rate Mahathmaya and J. T. Ellawela, after Maduwanwela had gone to see a kraal organised at Labugama in 1870 for the Duke of Edinburgh's visit; they chose it for the main stream and a perennial spring that elephants came to, and the stockade was built around the stream and the spring (Katugaha).

Construction detail from Katugaha: logs cut on the owner's own land; posts from the 1944 kraal tested and the sound ones reused; only every other upright fixed into the ground, to give the wall some yield under a charge; uprights ten feet apart; over a hundred men on the stockade with tame elephants placing logs; a post office and a police station established; the temporary settlement called Kraal Town, with camps for the Molamure, Elapata, Maduwanwela and Muttetuwegama parties and one for the Governor General; a blessing of the jungle deities performed beforehand with a mock stockade, dancers and kattandiyas.

The drive used around six hundred men and expressly forbade guns, firecrackers, drums and the banging of tin cans; each man had a stick to tap on trees, beaters worked in threes keeping night fires and singing pel kavi, the provided food was strictly vegetarian, and the herd was never allowed to stampede. Walalgoda Ralahamy was in charge of the drive (Katugaha).

The herd driven in consisted of sixteen elephants, with a few loners outside; two of the females were in oestrus; and one strong young bull went in with the herd (Katugaha). Seventeen animals inside the stockade is therefore the herd of sixteen plus that bull.
The young bull was mating with two of the females inside the stockade, one of them the matriarch, and became uncontrollable when the matriarch was tied to a tree (Katugaha).

He broke the hide ropes on two occasions, broke free from the hira gala, and broke a one-inch wire noose that had caught only half his foot and stuck between the nails, which irritated him further. Many tame elephants refused to face him; of three finally sent in, including the Mapitigama tusker, two fled and only Gunaya stood up to him and was knocked down and gored in the shoulder; Sir Francis drove the bull off with his 'charmed stick' (Katugaha, quoting Sam Elapata Jnr).
Release was considered and rejected as too dangerous, because a mating bull would not have left the area and both beaters and thousands of visitors were present (Katugaha).

No firearms were allowed in Kraal Town. Sam Kadirgama, Arthur Molamure and Shelton Ratwatte arrived at the site returning from a shoot, Kadirgama had a sufficiently powerful rifle, and Kadirgama shot the bull as it charged towards him; the hind legs buckled first, then the forelegs (Katugaha).

Katugaha states flatly that the newspapers' description was wrong: 'Though the News Papers screamed, "Tusker shot while defending the herd" it was not a tusker nor was he the leader of the herd. He was just a strong male that had joined the herd because of his sexual desires.'

Shooting elephants was not banned at the time. Katugaha: 'I must also state that the shooting of elephants was not banned at the time. They were shot in defence of crops and for "sport", with a license of course.'

There was much agitation about the 'unnecessary deaths' caused by these kraals, public opinion ran high, the matter was debated in Parliament, and Parliament passed a law banning elephant kraals; Katugaha's closing formulation is that the emotions expressed and the parliamentary debates 'finally led to the ban on Kraals, capture and killing of elephants'. He adds his own view that, given the declining numbers, 'this ban came at the correct time'.
The captured animals were sold at a public auction after noosing finished, buyers coming from far and wide, with a purchaser expected to take his animal away within five or six days (Katugaha).
Every adult elephant captured during the kraal, except the two tiny babies, had gunshot injuries (Katugaha, stated without comment).
The Governor General, Lord Soulbury, was present and was inside the stockade when an enraged female charged; Sam Elapata pushed him into a ditch and jumped in after him (Katugaha).

An Elephant Kraal Ordinance existed as a distinct instrument, and in its revised form it prohibits the kraaling of wild elephants, defined as capture by closing them in a stockade together with the activities of erecting one. The FAO/ECOLEX record gives it as 1912, revised 1955. The Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance's provisions referring to 'any elephant seized or taken at any elephant kraal held under the Elephant Kraal Ordinance' confirm that kraals were held under that separate ordinance.

Katugaha, writing in 2008, describes the site as follows: 'Panamure is but a memory now... The jungle itself is no more. Panamure is a developing town today. Just one or perhaps two of the upright post of the stockade are left and preserved in this town as historical mementos.'

The spring lies within the stream bed and is clearly visible only when the water level drops. It is reached by crossing the kraal ground to the stream and going about seventy metres upstream, taking the left branch at a Y junction and crossing one small tributary. Villagers hold it in regard and traditionally do not point directly at it when indicating where it is, and illegal gem working and a diverted stream are reported to have reduced its natural discharge (AmazingLanka).

The bull is remembered in popular memory under a royal title formed from the place name and the words for king of elephants, and books, a song and a memorial have followed. Widyarathne's 2016 academic abstract itself carries the emblematic version: 'the Majestic Panamure elephant made the history by sacrificing its life to protect 16 elephants in the herd.'
what_is_disputed: What the bull was. The scholarly account, from an author who had the story repeatedly from an organiser's family, says he was not a tusker and not the leader of the herd, but a strong young male that had joined the herd to mate. The contemporary press, the popular Sinhala literature, the nationalist reading and Widyarathne's 2016 academic abstract all make him the herd's leader, a tusker, and a sacrifice for his herd; one Sinhala account gives him a name and a height of about nine feet and has him resisting for four days. The film holds these apart and joins neither, and it records that a royal title was given without adopting it.

How many animals were driven in. Katugaha gives a herd of sixteen plus one young bull who ran in with them, with loners outside. The widely repeated figure is seventeen driven in. One popular Sinhala account gives twenty-seven. Seventeen is reconcilable with Katugaha only as sixteen plus the bull, and the film uses Katugaha's composition because the composition is the whole point of what happened.

The sequence of the noosing. Katugaha: noosed, hide ropes snapped twice, broke free from the hira gala, then a one-inch wire noose that took only half the foot and was broken with one kick. Popular accounts compress this to 'noosed twice with hide ropes, then broke a wire noose on a third attempt'. One widely repeated version has the trained elephants simply refusing to approach and a single rifle shot 'between the eyes'; Katugaha describes three tame elephants being sent in, two fleeing, one knocked down, and a shot whose effect he infers had reached the brain, without saying where it entered.

Who fired, and in what capacity. Katugaha names Sam Kadirgama, a visitor arriving back from a shoot with a suitable rifle. Sinhala sources and some English summaries describe him as a naval officer or Navy Commander, and the spelling varies (Kadirgama, Kadirgamar, Kadiragamr). Nothing found here establishes his position, and the film does not name him in narration.

The date. Popular accounts give the shooting as 10 August 1950, and a Daily Mirror seventy-fifth-anniversary piece published on 12 August 2025 is consistent with that. 9 August 1950 is also given. One Sinhala site gives 8 August 1950 for the drive and 5 August 1950 for the shooting, which is internally impossible. Katugaha gives no date at all beyond the year. The film's narration uses 10 August 1950 and the disagreement is recorded here.

The legislation: its date, its instrument and its scope. Katugaha says only that Parliament passed a law banning kraals, and then that the debates led to a ban on kraals, capture and killing; he names no statute and no year. Popular sources say the government 'introduced legislation prohibiting elephant kraals and restricting the capture and killing of elephants'. Other accounts date the ban on kraals to 1952. The FAO/ECOLEX record for the Elephant Kraal Ordinance gives 1912, revised 1955, with the revised text prohibiting kraaling. Conservation literature reports the 1950 measure more narrowly, as a ban on elephant captures by private individuals, and reports that private captures were permitted again in 1972-1974; that paper could not be read directly here and the claim is carried as reported, not verified. The three versions - a 1950 ban, a 1952 ban, and a 1955 revised ordinance - are not reconciled, and the narration therefore says that a law followed and the thing was not done again, which all sources support, rather than naming a statute.

The size of the owner's forest. 99,000 acres, about 40,065 hectares, is the figure in the popular sources and in Widyarathne's abstract. The biographical record gives the inheritance as 83,000 acres of timber and gem lands, and a related record in this project's own slate gives two royal grants totalling about 82,000 acres, of which the grant covering this ground is about 54,000. Nothing here resolves it and the film uses none of the figures.

How many people were involved. Katugaha gives over a hundred men on the stockade and around six hundred beaters on the drive. A 2016 newspaper account gives more than 1,800 persons building the stockade. The film uses Katugaha's six hundred for the drive, where his account is most detailed.

What is physically on the ground now. Katugaha in 2008: one or perhaps two upright posts, preserved in the town. A Sinhala site: the spring, an archaeological plaque, and a single wooden post re-erected by residents. A 2016 newspaper: 'Today, a monument honours this Tusker who fought to protect his herd.' A 2021 television report: the last kraal 'at the brink of destruction' through neglect. Sinhala coverage reports a foundation working on a museum and a life-size replica of the animal at the site. These cannot all describe the same ground in the same year and the site may have been built on since. Which of them is true in 2026 decides whether this film exists, and it is the first thing a pre-visit must settle.

The spring's behaviour. That the flow increased when elephants trumpeted near it, or when people spoke loudly nearby, is local tradition reported as tradition. The film may record that it is held and must not present it as fact or test it on camera.
A claim of a sixteen-hundred-year history of elephant dealing at the site appears in television coverage and is unsupported by anything found here. It is not used.

Above all, the meaning of the aftermath is not adjudicable from any of this and the film does not adjudicate it. The scholarly account's own tone is sceptical - 'All this hue and cry that was made on the death of one animal' - while also holding that the ban came at the right time. What the record establishes is that an act occurred, that public feeling followed it, that Parliament debated it and that a law ended the practice. It establishes nothing about whether anyone was right, culpable, redeemed or owed anything, and the film makes no such finding.

what_to_film: The whole clearing in one static wide in flat mid-morning light, from a position where the treeline and the line of the stream both read, held for minutes rather than seconds. This is the opening frame and the closing frame and the whole film is built to return to it.
A second static wide from a different position, level and unemphatic, across the part of the ground where the stockade line ran.
The stream at ground level: water over gravel, sand bars, the bank. Camera resting on the ground, no movement.
The spring in the stream bed, filmed only if the water is low enough to show it, at a distance that does not require anyone to enter or disturb it, and with the local observance respected.
The ground surface close and motionless: sand, root, gravel, ant path, leaf. No hand in frame.

Whatever marker, plaque, surviving upright or monument now stands on the site: one level frame at a normal distance, in the same light as everything else, or nothing at all. It is never the subject and is never filmed to be moving.
The edges of the ground in present-day ordinary use: a footpath, a fence line, a cultivated patch, the town audible behind the trees. Nobody identifiable, nobody performing.
A clean, thin ambient track over a long take with no wind: insects, water, one bird, a dog, a motorcycle behind the treeline. The sound has to carry the held frames.
suggested_location.access: By road. Reported as about 11.5 km from Embilipitiya on the Rakwana road, roughly thirty minutes, with the kraal ground beside the village; a related record in this project gives about 30 km from Embilipitiya along the same road to the manor at Kolonna, which is about 7 km further on. The ground itself appears to be walked onto, with the spring about seventy metres upstream of the crossing point, over a stream bed and one small tributary, so boots and a dry week matter more than a vehicle. Nothing about permission has been established. It is unclear who now owns or administers the ground, whether an archaeological designation applies, whether a foundation or local body controls access, and whether a museum or memorial project has enclosed any of it. Drone: uncertain, and not needed. A clearing reads perfectly well from the ground and this film is deliberately built without an aerial; if one establishing frame were wanted it would need its own civil aviation and local clearance, which has not been checked.
suggested_location.best_time: Dry weather, mid-morning to early afternoon, flat high light or thin overcast. The stream has to be low enough to show the spring in its bed, which points at the drier months; local accounts associate elephant visits historically with July to September dryness. A still day is required, because the ambient track has to carry very long static takes. Golden hour and rain are both wrong for this film.
suggested_location.research_note: The scholarly account was obtained and read in full: H. I. E. Katugaha, 'The Last Kraal in Sri Lanka', Gajah 29 (2008), pp. 5-10, downloaded as PDF from asesg.org and extracted page by page. It is the best source by a distance and it corrects the popular version in three places that matter. First, the animal: the newspapers ran 'Tusker shot while defending the herd' and Katugaha states flatly that he was neither a tusker nor the leader of the herd, but a strong young male that had joined the herd to mate and that was mating with the matriarch inside the stockade until she was tied to a tree. That single sentence dismantles the royal-title version of the event and it is why this film records that the title was given rather than using it. Second, the numbers: the herd was sixteen, with one young bull who ran in with it, not seventeen driven in as a herd. Third, the legality: shooting elephants was not banned at the time and was done under licence in defence of crops and for sport, which removes any basis for treating the organisers as lawbreakers. He also supplies the detail no popular account carries - the ten-foot post spacing and the deliberately unfixed alternate uprights, the ban on guns and drums during the drive, the vegetarian meals, the pel kavi singing, the public auction of the captives within five or six days, and the flat sentence that every adult captured except the two tiny babies already had gunshot injuries. His own tone about the aftermath is dry: 'All this hue and cry that was made on the death of one animal', followed by the judgement that the ban came at the right time. He gives no date for the kraal beyond the year and names no statute. Everything else here is desk research by web search and is unverified on the ground. The ownership and organisation were checked separately and the landowner is Sir Alexander Francis Molamure, first Speaker of the State Council and then of the Parliament of Ceylon, who died on 25 January 1951; the estate came to him from his uncle J. W. Maduwanwela, and the acreage figures disagree between sources and are not used. The date of the shooting, 10 August 1950, comes from popular accounts and is corroborated only circumstantially by a seventy-fifth-anniversary newspaper piece dated 12 August 2025; it is not in the scholarly paper and it is held in what_is_disputed. The legislation could not be pinned down: Katugaha names no statute, popular sources give 1950 and others 1952, the FAO/ECOLEX record for the Elephant Kraal Ordinance gives 1912 revised 1955 with the revised text prohibiting kraaling, and a conservation paper reporting a narrower 1950 ban on private captures with private captures resumed in 1972-1974 returned HTTP 403 and could not be read; that claim is carried as reported, not verified. The Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance text itself could not be retrieved, and the narration therefore says a law followed rather than naming one. Coordinates are the destination point given on a travel site's route from Embilipitiya and are not a surveyed position. What is physically on the ground is genuinely unresolved and is the single most important thing a pre-visit must settle: 2008 gives one or two surviving posts preserved in the town, a Sinhala site gives the spring plus an archaeological plaque plus one re-erected post, a 2016 newspaper says a monument now honours the animal, a 2021 television report calls the site close to destruction through neglect, and Sinhala coverage describes a foundation working towards a museum and a life-size replica. If a built attraction now occupies the ground, the absence this film is about no longer exists and the film should be dropped rather than adapted. Images are empty and that is a decision, not a gap. Wikimedia Commons holds nothing of this site: searches for the site name, the village, the spring and the district returned no photograph of the ground at all, and the only kraal material on Commons is colonial-era prints and plates of captures in progress - 'AMH-7006-KB Capturing elephants on Ceylon', 'AMH-7266-KB Elephant hunt on Ceylon' and an eighteenth-century Dutch plan, 'AMH-5362-NA Map of an elephant corral in the village of Welancoelaan' - all of which were rejected. The first two show animals being taken, which this film forbids outright; the third shows no animal but is a plan of a different stockade in a different century, and reproducing any stockade diagram would pull the record towards the reconstruction imagery the film exists to refuse. A photograph of some other village's landscape would be worse than none, so there is none. One structural note for Chathura: this location puts a third film of this group in the same district as two others, which is a concentration worth his eye even though the location itself is fixed.

unknowns: What is physically on the ground in 2026. The accounts disagree between one or two surviving posts, a plaque, a re-erected post, a monument, a site close to collapse through neglect, and a museum-and-replica project in progress. The film's whole subject is the absence, so this is the question that decides whether it can be made.
Who owns or administers the ground, whether any archaeological or local-authority designation applies, and from whom permission would be sought. No approach has been made to anyone.
Whether the spring is visible and reachable in the filming window, and how to film near it without breaching the local observance that surrounds it.

The exact date of the kraal and of the shooting, and the identity, date and scope of the legislation that followed. The narration is written so that neither has to be asserted beyond what the record supports.
Whether a drone can be flown here at all, and whether local sensitivity would make it inappropriate even if it were permitted. The film is built not to need one.
Whether the reported gem working in or near the stream bed is active, which affects both access and what the ground looks like.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified; the scholarly account behind the historical thread was obtained and read, and everything else is web research. No scene or shot is decided here.
